title: Northstar Finance x Redwood — Security review (Onboarding telemetry + retention)
summary: Northstar reviewed Redwood’s planned guided onboarding telemetry for the Hosted API checklist in Console. Redwood confirmed a strict “no customer prompt content” posture, a property allowlist, and redaction rules. Discussion covered event identity (org/project/user), whether IP/user agent are stored, retention windows for raw events vs aggregates, access controls (RBAC, least privilege), and customer options for auditability and deletion requests. Northstar’s main asks: written documentation of the event schema/properties, clear retention & deletion policy, and confirmation that telemetry can be disabled for their org when they move to a regulated environment (future VPC/Private). Redwood noted Phase 1 is self-serve Hosted API, but committed to share the v1 schema and the privacy review summary, and to confirm current opt-out controls / roadmap.
topics: What onboarding telemetry collects (event names + properties)
No prompt content / no PII-by-default guarantees and redaction
Retention: raw events vs derived aggregates; export/log access
Access controls, SOC 2 controls, and internal use (product analytics vs support)
Data residency considerations (US/EU) and regional routing
Customer requests: opt-out, deletion, and audit trails
questions: Do you store any prompt text, completion text, or embeddings in onboarding telemetry?
Do events include IP address, full user agent, or request/response payloads?
What is the retention period for raw event logs vs aggregated metrics?
Who inside Redwood can query onboarding telemetry (support, engineers, product)?
Can we disable onboarding telemetry collection for our org/project?
Can you support deletion requests tied to a user ID or org ID?
Is telemetry data processed in-region (EU) when using EU endpoints?
action_items: Redwood (Nadia Rahman) to send Northstar the onboarding telemetry event schema v1 (names + property allowlist + redaction rules).
Redwood (Michael Grant) to share a short written retention + access-control summary for onboarding telemetry (raw vs aggregates) suitable for privacy review.
Northstar (Elena Petrova) to confirm their internal retention requirement for product analytics (e.g., 30/90/365 days) and whether it differs for security logs.
Redwood (Logan Wright) to confirm whether IP/user-agent are stored in the onboarding telemetry pipeline and, if so, whether they are truncated/hashed and for how long.
Northstar (Sonia Iyer) to send Northstar’s standard telemetry / analytics security questionnaire (if different from their vendor intake).
Redwood (Marcus Lin) to follow up on telemetry opt-out / minimization options for regulated deployments and whether it can be scoped per-org.
next_steps: Redwood to email schema + privacy/retention summary by EOW
Northstar to review internally and come back with any required DPA/contract language
Schedule a 30-min follow-up if Northstar needs deeper data residency discussion
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Northstar Finance x Redwood — Security review (Onboarding telemetry + retention)
Date: 2026-02-19
Time: 4:00pm ET
Duration: 49 min
Attendees:
- Marcus Lin (Redwood Inference, Security Engineering)
- Michael Grant (Redwood Inference, Legal/Privacy)
- Logan Wright (Redwood Inference, Telemetry & Analytics Platform)
- Nadia Rahman (Redwood Inference, Event Schema & Pipelines)
- Sonia Iyer (Northstar Finance, Security Engineering)
- Ben Kline (Northstar Finance, Privacy Counsel)
- Ravi Deshpande (Northstar Finance, Platform Engineering)
- Elena Petrova (Northstar Finance, Data Governance)

(autogenerated) Summary:
Northstar asked detailed questions about Redwood’s “guided onboarding checklist” telemetry. Redwood confirmed: no prompt or completion content is collected in onboarding telemetry; properties are allowlisted; retention is bounded; and access is role-restricted.

(autogenerated) Topics:
- Telemetry properties and identity
- Retention and deletion
- Access controls
- Data residency

(autogenerated) Action items:
- Redwood to share schema + retention/access summary

Transcript:

[00:00] Marcus Lin: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making the time. This is Marcus, I’m on security engineering here at Redwood. Um, goal today is to walk through what we collect for the onboarding checklist telemetry, what we don’t collect, retention, and who can see it.

[00:17] Sonia Iyer: Great. Thanks Marcus. And just to set context, we’re evaluating your Hosted API first, but we need to be super clear about analytics and telemetry. We’ve gotten burned by vendors that say “no prompts” and then it turns out some debug logging caught payloads.

[00:32] Marcus Lin: Totally. We’ll be explicit. And if something is “it depends” we’ll call it out.

[00:37] Michael Grant: Michael here as well, privacy counsel. I can speak to policy/retention and contractual commitments.

[00:44] Logan Wright: Logan, I run the telemetry platform team.

[00:46] Nadia Rahman: And Nadia, I’m the one who wrote most of the event schema for this onboarding thing.

[00:52] Ravi Deshpande: Ravi, platform eng. I’m mostly interested in identity, IP collection, and whether it’s going to create a new data store we have to assess.

[01:00] Elena Petrova: Elena, governance. Retention, deletion, and access controls.

[01:06] Marcus Lin: Perfect. So first, what is this? It’s telemetry emitted when a user interacts with the Redwood Console onboarding checklist, like “created API key”, “made first successful request”, “visited usage dashboard” — stuff like that.

[01:23] Sonia Iyer: When you say “made first successful request,” that sounds like you’re inspecting requests?

[01:29] Logan Wright: Good question. It’s not the request body. It’s derived from gateway metrics/logs that already exist for operating the API. The validator basically checks for a 2xx for the project, and then marks the checklist step complete.

[01:44] Nadia Rahman: Yeah, the event is like `onboarding.step_completed` with `step_id=first_successful_request` and then some identifiers.

[01:54] Ben Kline: Okay. Let’s just do the big one first: do you store prompt text, completion text, embeddings, tool arguments — any customer content — in this onboarding telemetry stream?

[02:05] Marcus Lin: In onboarding telemetry specifically: no. We have a “no customer prompt content” constraint in the design. There is a property allowlist — only specific keys are permitted. Anything else is dropped.

[02:17] Ben Kline: Dropped where? Client-side? Server-side?

[02:20] Nadia Rahman: Both, kinda. The Console has a typed event interface and it won’t compile if you add random properties — but we don’t rely on that. Server-side ingestion enforces an allowlist again. If a property isn’t on the list, it gets removed.

[02:39] Ravi Deshpande: Does it log the full payload before stripping? Like, does it hit an API gateway log with the original JSON?

[02:47] Logan Wright: The ingestion endpoint logs are configured not to log request bodies. We log status code, latency, route, request id. Not the payload.

[02:56] Sonia Iyer: I want that in writing, just FYI.

[02:58] Michael Grant: Yep, we can summarize that in our written response.

[03:02] Elena Petrova: What identifiers are included in the telemetry events? User identifiers can become personal data for us.

[03:09] Nadia Rahman: The required identity fields are `org_id` and `project_id`. We also include a `user_id` which is the Redwood Console user (so, your employees) and a `session_id`. There’s also an `event_id` and a `dedupe_key`.

[03:27] Ben Kline: Is `user_id` an email address?

[03:29] Nadia Rahman: No, it’s an internal UUID. We do not include email in the event payload.

[03:35] Marcus Lin: And to be clear, we do have user profile data in our auth system, but onboarding telemetry events don’t include those attributes.

[03:43] Ravi Deshpande: How about IP address?

[03:46] Logan Wright: For onboarding telemetry events, we don’t store IP as an event property. There may be standard infrastructure logs at the edge that have IP for security purposes, but that’s not in the analytics event stream.

[03:58] Sonia Iyer: “May be” is the part that makes me nervous.

[04:01] Marcus Lin: Totally fair. Let’s separate: (1) product analytics events for onboarding; (2) security/operational logs for the API and Console. For (1), no IP. For (2), we do have standard access logs, and those have IPs for abuse detection, rate limiting investigation, etc.

[04:20] Elena Petrova: And retention differs between (1) and (2)?

[04:24] Logan Wright: Yes.

[04:26] Ben Kline: Can you state retention for the onboarding telemetry events?

[04:30] Logan Wright: Current plan: raw onboarding events retained for 90 days in our event store. Aggregated metrics (like funnel counts by day) kept longer — about 13 months — so we can do year-over-year, seasonality, that type of thing.

[04:49] Elena Petrova: 90 days raw, 13 months aggregates. Who can query raw?

[04:54] Logan Wright: Limited set. Analytics team and oncall engineers for the telemetry pipeline, plus some product analytics users. It’s behind RBAC and audited. Support does not have direct query access.

[05:09] Sonia Iyer: But support can request someone else to look it up.

[05:12] Marcus Lin: They can file an internal request, yes, but they don’t have self-serve access. That’s an intentional control.

[05:19] Ben Kline: Are those access events logged? Like, if someone runs a query on our org_id, is there an audit trail?

[05:26] Logan Wright: We log access to the warehouse and we log admin actions. For ad-hoc queries, the query itself is logged. Whether it’s “human readable audit” is… it’s query logs, but yes, we have an audit trail.

[05:44] Ravi Deshpande: Does the onboarding telemetry ever include request IDs that could be used to correlate back to API logs that might contain more?

[05:52] Nadia Rahman: There’s a `request_id` field for some validators, but it’s optional. For example, “first successful request” step completion might include the gateway request id for debugging. That request id does not contain payload, it’s just a token.

[06:09] Sonia Iyer: That’s still correlatable, though.

[06:12] Marcus Lin: It is, but correlation would be within our systems. And again, the API logs we keep don’t have payload bodies. So the chain doesn’t lead to prompt content.

[06:25] Ben Kline: Do you have any exceptions where prompt content is stored anywhere, for any reason? Like “customer opted in to share prompts for evaluation.”

[06:33] Marcus Lin: Not by default. Some customers run evals and can upload prompt sets into the product, but that’s a separate feature with explicit user action and separate storage. That’s not this onboarding telemetry stream.

[06:48] Elena Petrova: For the onboarding checklist, do you record which docs links people click? UTM parameters, URLs can sometimes contain internal names.

[06:56] Nadia Rahman: We track “docs link clicked” for a couple steps, but the property is a canonical doc slug, not the full URL. And we’re standardizing UTMs to be like `utm_source=console&utm_campaign=onboarding&utm_content=step_<id>`. We avoid passing user-entered query params.

[07:16] Ravi Deshpande: So you’re not collecting full referrer.

[07:18] Logan Wright: Not in the event. The browser itself has referrer headers, but again, our telemetry event payload doesn’t include it.

[07:28] Sonia Iyer: Can we get the full list of event names and properties? Like literally the schema.

[07:33] Nadia Rahman: Yes. We have a v1 schema doc. I’ll send it. It enumerates event names like `onboarding.checklist_viewed`, `onboarding.step_started`, `onboarding.step_completed`, `onboarding.step_failed_validation` — and the required/optional properties.

[07:50] Ben Kline: Great. In particular, we’ll look for anything that could be considered personal data — user agent strings, locale, IP, etc.

[07:58] Marcus Lin: Understood.

[08:01] Sonia Iyer: Data residency: we’re primarily US, but we have EU users. Does Console telemetry route to the US only?

[08:09] Logan Wright: Today, our analytics pipeline is US-based. For hosted inference requests, we have region options. For Console telemetry, it’s currently centralized.

[08:20] Sonia Iyer: That’s potentially a blocker for us in the EU.

[08:23] Michael Grant: We should separate what’s required for you now versus what you’d require at scale. For onboarding telemetry, it’s minimal, but yes, it’s still data.

[08:33] Ben Kline: If it’s user IDs of EU employees, that’s personal data. So, yes, we care.

[08:38] Marcus Lin: Totally. For Phase 1, we don’t have EU-local analytics processing. We can document where it’s processed and ensure it’s covered under our DPA and SCCs.

[08:50] Elena Petrova: Can we opt out of onboarding telemetry?

[08:54] Logan Wright: For the feature itself, it’s behind a feature flag. If you don’t enable the checklist, you won’t generate those UI events. But baseline operational logs still exist.

[09:06] Ravi Deshpande: But the validators for “first successful request” — that’s based on gateway logs — those still happen.

[09:10] Logan Wright: Correct.

[09:12] Sonia Iyer: We’d need an explicit “disable analytics” for our org, not just “don’t show UI.”

[09:18] Marcus Lin: I hear you. For this specific onboarding telemetry stream, we can likely implement an org-level suppression. I don’t want to promise it’s live today. But it’s a reasonable request.

[09:31] Nadia Rahman: Also, we already tag events with `org_id`, so suppression is feasible at ingestion.

[09:38] Ben Kline: Deletion: If one of our users requests deletion, can you delete events associated with their user id?

[09:45] Logan Wright: In raw events, yes, we can run a deletion job by `user_id` or `org_id`. For aggregates, it’s more complicated because they’re rolled up, but they’re not user-level.

[09:59] Elena Petrova: You’re saying aggregates are not keyed by user.

[10:02] Logan Wright: Correct. Aggregates are like “step completion count per day per cohort.” Not “Sonia completed step.”

[10:10] Sonia Iyer: What about dashboards your product team uses — can they drill down to individual orgs?

[10:16] Logan Wright: Yes, there are filters by org_id for debugging rollout issues, but access is restricted. Most product views are cohort-level.

[10:26] Marcus Lin: And we’re adding alerts for missing events, pipeline delays, and sudden drop-offs — again, those are aggregated and operational.

[10:36] Ravi Deshpande: Can you talk about encryption? At rest, in transit.

[10:40] Marcus Lin: In transit TLS. At rest encrypted. Keys are managed by our cloud KMS. Access is via IAM roles, with least privilege.

[10:50] Sonia Iyer: SOC 2?

[10:52] Marcus Lin: We are SOC 2 Type II. We can share the report under NDA.

[10:58] Ben Kline: Please do, and also clarify whether this telemetry store is in-scope for SOC 2.

[11:05] Marcus Lin: It is in-scope as part of our production systems; we’ll confirm in the follow-up email.

[11:12] Nadia Rahman: One more detail: we have a “property allowlist” plus a “sensitive value detector.” If something looks like an email address or credit card pattern, it’s redacted. It’s like belt-and-suspenders.

[11:28] Sonia Iyer: That’s good. But those detectors can be imperfect. So the primary control is “don’t collect.”

[11:34] Nadia Rahman: Exactly.

[11:36] (crosstalk)

[11:37] Elena Petrova: How do you prevent engineers from adding new properties ad hoc?

[11:42] Logan Wright: Schema changes go through review. We have a code-owned registry; Nadia’s team and security review changes. It’s not “any engineer can add fields.”

[11:53] Marcus Lin: Also, for onboarding specifically, security asked for “no prompt content” as a non-negotiable. So any schema additions that touch request data would be rejected.

[12:06] Ben Kline: Can you speak to the boundary between onboarding telemetry and the broader usage analytics? Like token counts and such.

[12:14] Logan Wright: Usage analytics for billing uses metering events: token counts, model, latency, status code, project. No prompts. That data is retained longer for invoicing reasons. Onboarding telemetry is separate.

[12:30] Ravi Deshpande: Is there any chance that “structured output” or “tool calling” parameters get into logs?

[12:37] Marcus Lin: Not in onboarding telemetry. For API request logs, again we don’t log bodies. We do log high-level route names and status.

[12:47] Sonia Iyer: What about error traces? Sometimes a 500 captures request context.

[12:52] Marcus Lin: Good catch. Application errors can include stack traces. We have guards to avoid including request bodies in error reporting. It’s something we audit because it’s easy to make mistakes.

[13:06] Ben Kline: Okay.

[13:08] Elena Petrova: Let’s go back to retention. 90 days raw — is that configurable per customer?

[13:14] Michael Grant: Not today for self-serve hosted. For enterprise contracts, we can discuss. But the baseline is uniform.

[13:25] Sonia Iyer: We’d prefer 30 days raw.

[13:28] Logan Wright: We can take that as feedback. The reason for 90 is debugging and comparing cohorts. But if we need to reduce for certain accounts, we can explore.

[13:41] Ravi Deshpande: Are you sampling events?

[13:44] Nadia Rahman: For onboarding telemetry, no sampling. It’s low volume and we need accurate funnel metrics.

[13:53] Sonia Iyer: Then it’s definitely personal data volume for us.

[13:56] Marcus Lin: Understood.

[14:00] Ben Kline: For lawful basis, we’ll treat it as vendor processing. We need DPA language and SCCs if data goes from EU to US.

[14:08] Michael Grant: We have standard DPA and SCCs. We’ll include those in the package.

[14:14] Sonia Iyer: One more question: does the onboarding checklist itself ever display customer-specific names inside the telemetry event? Like “step name includes project name.”

[14:24] Nadia Rahman: No, step IDs are fixed enumerations. We don’t include project name. We include `project_id`.

[14:31] Ravi Deshpande: Okay. And do you include model names?

[14:35] Nadia Rahman: Some events include `model_id` when the step is “try streaming” or “try structured output.” It’s a Redwood model identifier like `rw-...` not the prompt.

[14:47] Sonia Iyer: That’s fine.

[14:49] Elena Petrova: How about internal ticketing — if support escalates, do they paste telemetry into Slack?

[14:55] Marcus Lin: We train against copying sensitive customer data into Slack. For onboarding telemetry, the only data would be IDs and timestamps. But yes, operationally, humans can make mistakes; we have policies and logging.

[15:12] Sonia Iyer: Okay.

[15:14] Ben Kline: Let’s talk about “no customer prompt content” again. Is that a contractual commitment you can make? Not just “best effort.”

[15:22] Michael Grant: We can commit that we do not collect or store customer prompt content in onboarding telemetry, and more broadly we have commitments about not using customer content for training absent explicit opt-in. We’ll put the relevant language in the DPA / terms.

[15:39] Sonia Iyer: Good.

[15:41] Ravi Deshpande: Are there any third parties involved? Segment, Amplitude, etc.

[15:47] Logan Wright: For onboarding telemetry, we do not send to third-party analytics. It’s first-party pipeline.

[15:54] Ben Kline: That’s helpful.

[15:56] Elena Petrova: Who is the data controller/processor in this context?

[16:00] Michael Grant: For the telemetry associated with your account/users, Redwood is a processor; you’re the controller. We’ll reflect that in the DPA.

[16:10] Sonia Iyer: Alright. I think the main follow-ups are: schema, retention/access write-up, and confirm IP handling.

[16:18] Marcus Lin: Yep, we captured those.

[16:20] Logan Wright: I’ll double-check the IP/user-agent topic. I’m pretty sure it’s not in the event properties, but I want to confirm what’s in the edge logs and how long those are retained.

[16:32] Ben Kline: And for data residency, we’ll need a written statement of where onboarding telemetry is stored.

[16:38] Marcus Lin: We can provide that. Today, US. If you require EU-only, that’s a roadmap conversation.

[16:47] Sonia Iyer: Okay. Thanks.

[16:49] Marcus Lin: Before we wrap, any last questions?

[16:52] Elena Petrova: If we become a customer, can we get a list of sub-processors?

[16:56] Michael Grant: Yes, standard sub-processor list and change notification.

[17:01] Sonia Iyer: Great. Let’s do that.

[17:04] Marcus Lin: Cool. We’ll send the follow-up email. Thanks all.

[17:08] (Meeting ends — transcript continued with minor hallway chat)

[17:09] Ravi Deshpande: Thanks.

[17:10] Ben Kline: Thank you.
